title: Animalogic
description:
Examining the nature of the beast.

Why do animals look, act, and evolve the way they do? Animalogic is a deep dive into the biology, behavior, and evolutionary logic of the creatures we share this planet with, from the ones that terrify us to the ones we've never even heard of.

We don't do surface-level. Every episode breaks down the science behind what makes an animal what it is: how it kills, how it survives, how it got that way, and what it tells us about life on Earth.

New episodes weekly. Stay curious, stay wild. 🌿

episodes.title: There's No Such Thing As A Giraffe
episodes.description:
There is no such thing as the giraffe. Not one species — four.

For 267 years, science treated every giraffe on the continent as one animal wearing different coats. Then genome sequencing quietly took that apart. In August 2025, the IUCN officially recognized four separate giraffe species, split not by looks, but by DNA that had been diverging in isolation for over 200,000 years, hidden behind rivers, rift valleys and rainforest the animals never crossed.

In this episode, we follow the genetic trail that undid two centuries of assumption — and the surprisingly human argument over what a "species" even is. We also get into how a 2-metre trachea keeps giraffes almost silent, why their necks may have evolved for combat rather than reaching leaves, and why splitting one giraffe into four turns a "vulnerable" animal into one, the Northern giraffe, quietly down over 80% in 35 years and easy to miss entirely.

The giraffe has been standing in plain sight the whole time. We just weren't counting it right.

episodes.description:
Everyone's favourite egg-laying little freak, the platypus, might be lying to us. Not about laying eggs, but about its evolution, and what it means for our own.

Every science book says it's a relic, a mammal that never got the memo to switch to live birth like the rest of us. But a new fossil discovery tells us this story might be backwards: our own branch of the family tree may have jumped from egg to live birth, back to egg, and then back to live birth again, but the platypus just didn't have time for that, and stayed eggy.

We reviewed all the evidence and the biggest mysteries in live birth evolution. So today we're asking: could the platypus be an innovative luddite that changed back to laying eggs, and not the mammal that didn't catch up? And could it happen again?

episodes.title: We Were Wrong About What's Killing Monarchs
episodes.description:

episodes.title: What the “American Cheetah” Actually Was
episodes.description:
For decades, we've pictured miracinonyx, or the American cheetahs, as fleet-footed prairie hunters who chased down pronghorns and were among the fastest animals on Earth. But recent studies have shaken that belief to the core. Thanks to fossils found in rocky canyons and subarctic lands, and studies on their diet, we're beginning to get a clearer picture of what these majestic animals actually were.

episodes.title: Meet the Caiman Bigger Than a T-Rex
episodes.description:
The purussaurus was the largest caiman that ever lived and ruled a massive swamp in what is now the Amazon rainforest. At first its body made no sense. It was simply too big and hunting prey would have been tough. It's hard to sneak up to prey when you're the size of a bus. But recent evidence shows that it did hunt and captured prey with amazing precision, going for the face when they approached the lake for a sip of water. This caiman was scarier than the creature of the black lagoon. It was the real Amazonian swamp monster.
